Achievement badges are a funny thing. You know they’re just a simple little bit of visual flair, they don’t even do anything, and yet for some reason you just have to collect them. Gamification can be a great motivator, and the achievement badges for the activity tracking on the Apple Watch have inspired many users to get more exercise.

If you want to maximize your badge count, you’re going to want to chase down as many activity achievements as you can. Most are available year-round, but there are also some time-limited special events to grab, too. Here’s a list of all the activity achievements for the Apple Watch and how to unlock them.

Standard achievements

Most of the achievements can be earned year-round. If you open the Activity app on your iPhone, then head over to the Achievements tab, you’ll see some of them listed even before you earn them (in which case they will be represented by a grey outline).

However, there are some achievements that are not shown until you earn them. Past and future monthly challenges, for example, won’t show up, nor do all the various individual exercise workouts.

Here is a list of all the standard badges you can get.

First [exercise] Workout

The first time you perform a new exercise for at least 5 minutes, you’ll get a achievement badge. Every workout type that does not fall under the “Other” category is eligible for this badge: from walking to yoga to HIIT to hiking and more.

Activities with both indoor and outdoor variants, like Cycling and Walking, are bundled together; you can do either activity to get the badge, and can only get it once.

[exercise] Workout Record

Every time you beat your previous best record for calories burned in any of the exercises listed above, you get this badge.

There is one caveat: You must complete five workouts of that type first. If you want to game the system, make sure your first four workouts of each type are short and easy, so it won’t take much effort to beat them.

7-Workout Week

Simply complete any workout of at least 15 minutes every day of the week. Note that the week is Monday-Sunday, and you have to do a workout on each of those days (you can’t simply do any seven days in a row). If you start a walking workout whenever you walk outside, you can achieve this easily.

New Move Record

Any day that your Move ring goes further than ever before (meaning you burned more calories in a day), you’ll earn this award. There’s one catch: you have to use your Apple Watch for 10 days before you can complete this.

New Exercise Record

This is just like the Move Record achievement, only for the green ring. This one is based on minutes of exercise, not calories burned, so it’s really easy to get. Just like the Move Record achievement, you have to use your Apple Watch for 10 days first.

Move Goal 200%, 300%, 400%

You earn this when you exceed your calorie target (the red Move ring) by 2x, 3x, or 4x, respectively. In other words, it’s given for making the red activity ring go around two, three, or four times in a day. It’s easy to get if you just set your Move goal very low.

New Move Goal

Every time you change your daily Move goal, and then exceed that new goal, you get this achievement. You can change your Move goal by opening the Activity app on your Apple Watch and force-pressing the screen.

Longest Move Streak

When you hit your Move goal (close the red ring) several days in a row, that’s a “streak.” You get this award when your streak finally ends, if it’s longer than your previous best streak.

Perfect Week

This is given out for four categories: Move, Exercise, Stand, and All Activity. For the first three, simply close the rings (red, green, or blue) every day of the week. To get the Perfect Week (All Activity) badge, close all three rings every day for an entire week. You can earn this multiple times, though it only shows one badge.

Remember, one week in the Activity app is from Monday-Sunday!

Perfect Month

Unlike Perfect Week, there are not multiple different Perfect Month badges for the different color rings. The lone Perfect Month achievement is for closing the red Move ring every day of the month.

There’s a separate Perfect Month badge for every month and every year, though. So you can earn this in February and again in March, and again in February in the next year.

Monthly Challenge

Each month has its own unique fitness challenge. If you have notifications set for the Activity app on our Apple Watch, you’ll see the goal presented at the beginning of the month, but you’ll also see the current month’s challenge in the Achievements tab of the Activity app on your iPhone. It will be a grey outline before it’s completed, but you can tap on it to see what the challenge entails.

The monthly challenge may task you with burning a specific number of calories, working out a number of times, or traveling a certain distance. There’s no telling what each new month will bring, you just have to look!

100, 365, 500, 1,000 Move Goals

When you hit your daily Move goal (close the red ring) 100 times, you get an achievement badge. You get another for hitting it 365 times, 500 times, and 1,000 times. These do not need to be in a row; it’s just the total number of times you’ve ever hit the goal.

Limited Achievements

Apple offers multiple one-off challenges per year that are only available for a limited time. Often, they’re only around for one day or one weekend. Some are limited to the U.S. because they’re based on U.S. holidays.

You’ll get a notification on your Apple Watch when one of them is coming up (make sure you have notifications enabled for the Activity app, using the Watch app on your iPhone).

Earning this award is a walk in the park. Or a run. Or a hike. Or a wheelchair push. Just record one of these workouts for 20 minutes or more on August 23.

Apple has begun beta testing for iOS and iPadOS 27.3, along with the 27.3 versions of all its other operating systems. This release should bring early Apple Intelligence features to China, as well as the Audio Intelligence features of Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, the redesigned Health app, and new Siri AI features within apps.

We expect the final public release will take place sometime near the end of November or early December.

What’s new in the iOS 27.3 beta

Here are some of the new features and changes discovered in the iOS 27.3 beta so far:

New Health app: The newly-designed Health app is back, after a brief appearance in the 27.2 betas.

Audio Intelligence: Together with an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, the Live Rewind and Siri Recap features are now available. Read more about privacy with these features here.

Safari features: Safari gets vertical tabs, Siri AI actions, and adaptive dark mode. Read more about these feautres here.

Siri AI languages: Siri AI expands to Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

iPhone Duo Reachability: An accessibility feature made to shift content to the side on the iPhone Duo, so it’s easier to reach on the extra-wide phone.

Apple Intelligence in China: China gets some basic Apple Intelligence features like Writing Tools, Visual Intelligence, Clean Up, Genmoji, and more. Siri AI is not available.

Fitness+ Gym Strength: New features in Fitness+ to build a gym strength training plan including the ability to track reps and weight.

StandBy updates: On regular iPhones, StandBy mode has more of the options and configurability found on iPhone Duo. It still only works when your iPhone is charging, unlike iPhone Duo.

Siri actions in Apple apps: Siri gets a lot of new capabilites across Apple apps like Calendar, Music, Messages, Reminders, Weather, and more. You can ask Siri what it can do in each app.

Siri actions in third-party apps: The 27.3 developer previews add App Intents for developers that allow them to integrate their content and actions into Siri. So data from third-party apps can be part of your “personal context” and you can use natural language to have Siri perform actions in those apps (once they are updated to do so).

iOS 27.3: How to install

If you want to test the iOS 27 beta releases but are not a registered developer, follow these steps:

  1. Click Sign Up on the Apple Beta page and register with your Apple ID.
  2. Log in to the Beta Software Program.
  3. Click Enroll your iOS device.
  4. Open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update.
  5. In the Beta Updates section, select the iOS Public Beta.

It may take a few moments after registering for the beta option to appear in Software Update.

iOS 27.3: How to install the developer beta

You’ll need to be registered as an Apple developer, but a free developer account will do. You can get one via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app:

  1. Download the Apple Developer App from the App Store.
  2. Open the app.
  3. Tap on Account.
  4. Sign in using your usual Apple ID.

Apple released macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14, 2026, but development hasn’t stopped. The latest update, macOS 27.2, became publicly available on October 26, completing its beta cycle.

The newest beta is macOS 27.3. The developer beta became available on November 3, 2026. The public beta will likely become available once beta 2 is ready.

Beta releases give developers and testers early access to upcoming features, fixes and refinements. However, unfinished software can introduce bugs, compatibility problems and increased battery drain, so we recommend caution – particularly if you rely on your Mac for work.

This guide tracks developer and public beta availability, explains what’s new, and helps you decide whether to participate. You’ll also find installation instructions, advice on reducing the risks, and guidance on returning to a public release.

What’s the latest macOS beta?

Apple offers two beta streams: a developer beta and a public beta. The public beta allows enthusiasts and early adopters to test upcoming changes before they are released to everyone. You need to join Apple’s Beta Software Program to access it.

  • Latest public release: macOS 27.3 beta 1, released November 3, 2026.
  • Previous beta cycle: macOS 27.2 Release Candidate on October 19, 2026.
  • Next developer or public beta: macOS 27.3 beta 2 release date to be determined, like a week after beta 1.

macOS 26 Tahoe beta: Apple may continue updating macOS 26 Tahoe with security and maintenance releases, but macOS 27 is now the current operating system and the focus of Apple’s beta program.

macOS 27 Beta timeline

What’s new in the latest beta?

Foundry

Apple has not announced the next beta, but as we become aware of major consumer-facing additions in macOS 27.3 beta we will list them here.

The following changes are expected, though:

  • Safari: new features include vertical tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI implementation. Learn more.
  • Bug fixes and performance improvements: Addressing issues in macOS 27.
  • Additional Siri AI languages: Apple has said the Siri AI will expand to Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese by the end of 2026.
  • Automatic password changes: The promised feature that will identify weak or compromised credentials and direct users to the appropriate website to change them has not yet been implemented, but it could arrive in macOS 27.3.

We’ll update this section as changes are discovered.

See Apple’s developer website for more information about the beta.

Should you install the macOS beta?

Apple

Installing the macOS beta lets you test Apple’s next round of features, fixes and refinements before their public release. Most Mac users should remain on the standard version of macOS 27, particularly if they rely on their Mac for work.

Install if…

  • You need to test apps
  • You want early access to new features
  • You have a secondary Mac available

Wait if…

  • This is your primary work machine
  • You rely on niche or specialist software
  • Stability is critical to your workflow

What are the risks of installing beta software?

Installing pre-release software on a primary device carries several risks.

  • System instability: Performance problems, freezes, crashes, and other unexpected behavior are common during beta testing.
  • App failures: Third-party applications may crash, behave unpredictably, or stop working entirely.
  • Hardware strain: Early beta builds can increase battery drain and cause Macs to run hotter than usual.
  • Data loss: Software bugs may corrupt files, and downgrading to a stable version often requires a complete system reset.

Safety precautions and best practices

If you decide to install the beta, take the following precautions:

  • Use a secondary device: Avoid installing beta software on your primary Mac or on any machine used for critical work.
  • Create a full backup: Use Time Machine to create a complete backup before upgrading so you can restore your Mac if something goes wrong. Note that this needs to be a Time Machine backup from before the beta was installed and you will lose anything saved subsequently.
  • Install on a separate volume: Consider installing the beta on a separate volume or external SSD rather than replacing your main operating system.
  • Check storage space: Make sure you have at least 15GB of free storage available before beginning the installation.

How to install the macOS beta

Foundry

The process for installing a macOS beta depends on whether you are seeking the Developer Beta or the Public Beta. Apple simplified this process a few years ago, removing the need for a paid developer account to access early builds.

The first step is to join Apple’s beta testing program. We explain how to do that in a separate article.

You will need to register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac.

To install the beta follow these steps:

  1. Back up your Mac: Before installing any pre-release software, it is critical to prepare your Mac to avoid data loss. Beta software is inherently unstable and can cause crashes or app compatibility issues.
  2. Register your account either as a public beta tester or as a developer in order to enable beta updates on your Mac:
    For the Public Beta: Visit the Apple Beta Software Program website, sign in with your Apple ID, and agree to the terms.
    For the Developer Beta: Register as an Apple Developer on Apple’s website, download the Apple Developer app from the App Store, sign in with your standard Apple ID, and complete the free registration process.
  3. On the Mac where you wish to install the beta, open System Settings and navigate to General > Software Update.
  4. Click the (i) info button next to Beta Updates.
  5. Enable Beta Updates.
  6. The beta will appear as an available upgrade. Select the macOS beta you want to install (e.g., macOS Public Beta or Developer Beta).
  7. Click Upgrade Now to begin the download and installation.

As long as you are a registered developer or enrolled in the public beta program, when the relevant macOS Beta becomes available, it will also show up on your Mac.

Once you are running the beta, the updates will come through to your Mac automatically; you just need to go to Software Update in System Settings and click to install. See How to install macOS.

How to get a free Apple developer account

If you just want a free Apple Developer account so you can access the beta, you can get this via Xcode or the Apple Developer app in iOS. Here’s how to do it via the Apple Developer app on an iPhone:

  1. Get the Apple Developer App from the App Store. 
  2. Open the app on your iPhone. 
  3. Tap on Account. 
  4. Tap on Sign In. 
  5. Sign in using your usual Apple ID. 

If you wish to actually publish applications to the App Store or receive support, you’ll need to pay $99/£79 per year for a paid account. You can compare the free and paid accounts here.

FAQ

1.

Who can run the macOS beta?

Anyone can run the macOS beta, but to do so, you do need to register for either the developer beta, the public beta, or both.

Apple offers both developer and public beta programs for macOS, enabling all interested users to test pre-release versions of the operating system. While both betas provide early access to new features, they cater to different user profiles based on technical expertise and risk tolerance. Beta software tends to be buggy so the more stable public beta version may be preferable, but even that will not be bug-free.

In the past, the developer beta was only available to developers who had paid to join Apple’s Developer Program (which costs $99/£79). However, for a couple of years now, Apple has opened up the developer beta to registered developers with free developer accounts. We explain how to get a free developer account below.

If you decide you no longer want to run the beta version of macOS read this: How to remove the macOS beta.

2.

macOS public beta vs developer beta

Since 2023, the Developer Beta has been available to anyone who registers as a developer, even if they aren’t a paid-up member of Apple’s Developer Program. As a result, people with a basic free developer account can download the new macOS developer beta (we show you how to register below).

Whether you should download the developer beta if you aren’t a developer is another question. We don’t recommend you install the developer beta if you aren’t a developer. Instead, our recommendation is to use the public beta (the first version of which usually arrives in July).

There are a few differences between the public and developer betas. The public beta is not the same as the beta that is released through the developer program. The public beta typically launches after the developer beta has undergone initial testing and refinement

Developers get updates to their beta first, and possibly more frequently. But you should keep in mind that betas are by nature not stable, and because the public beta comes after the developer beta it could be a little safer to install.

The most significant difference is probably the motive of the testers: Developers usually have the aim of ensuring their apps work when the updated macOS is released to the general public, while public beta testers are essentially helping Apple detect bugs and offering feedback on the features. Because of this, developers may get to test new features not available in the public beta. 

If you want to get the public beta the first thing you need to do, if you haven’t already, is join Apple’s beta programs read this for more information: How to become an Apple beta tester.

3.

Is the macOS beta stable?

By its nature, a beta has the potential to be unstable. Therefore, it’s not advised that you install it on a Mac that you rely on. If you have a second Mac that isn’t mission-critical, then install it there. We strongly recommend that you don’t risk all by putting the macOS beta on your primary Mac, especially not in the early days of the beta development. 

If you don’t have a second Mac, there are a couple of ways you could run macOS beta on your Mac without running the risk of losing data or finding your Mac stops working:

  • We recommend installing it on a partition, which these days is really a volume (and is much easier to create than a partition was). Read about how to do that here: How to dual-boot Mac: Run two versions of macOS on a Mac.
  • Alternatively, you could install the macOS beta on an external drive and run it on that.

We discuss the safety of the macOS beta and the risks you might be taking in more detail in a separate article.

4.

How to prepare your Mac for the beta

Update your software: We recommend you have the latest full version of macOS installed, although Apple says that the macOS Developer Beta Access Utility requires macOS 10.8 or later.

Make space: We’d recommend at least 25-30GB of available space because the macOS betas tend to be very large. If you end up requiring more space, read: How to free up space on Mac. Note that we always recommend that you have at least 10% space free on your Mac at any time, so if you don’t have that, expect problems!

Back up: Before you install a beta on your Mac, you should make a backup of your data and files. You can find out how to use Time Machine to back up your Mac. We also have a round-up of suitable backup solutions.

5.

How to send feedback to Apple

Should you come across an error or a bug, you should use the Feedback Assistant app to provide feedback to Apple. Launch the app and follow the appropriate steps, selecting the area about which you’re providing feedback and then any specific sub-area. Then describe your issue in a single sentence, before providing a more detailed description, including any specific steps that reproduce the issue. You’ll also be able to attach other files.

You’ll also have to give permission for the Feedback Assistant app to collect diagnostic information from your Mac.

It won’t always be obvious whether something is a bug or just not as easy to use as you might have hoped. Either way, if your feedback is that something appears to work in an illogical way, Apple will want to know that.

If you are having trouble with a third-party app, you can let Apple know by reporting it through the 3rd-party Application Compatibility category in the Feedback Assistant. However, we’d suggest that you also provide feedback to the app’s developer, who will no doubt be grateful.

6.

Will I be able to update from macOS beta to the final version?

Beta users can move to the finished release once its build is newer than – or equivalent to – the beta installed. Read: How to leave the macOS beta.

7.

Can I talk about the beta publicly?

According to Apple and the license agreement all beta testers must agree to, the beta is “Apple confidential information”. By accepting those terms, you agree not to discuss your use of the software with anyone who isn’t also in the Beta Software Program. That means you can’t “blog, post screenshots, tweet, or publicly post information about the public beta software.”

However, you can discuss any information that Apple has publicly disclosed; the company says that information is no longer considered confidential.

8.

How to downgrade from the macOS beta

You can always revert to an earlier version of macOS, though depending on how you back up, it’s not necessarily a painless process.

Start by making sure the data on your drive is backed up, then erase the drive and install the latest public version of macOS. When you first start up your Mac, you can use the Migration Assistant to import your data from the backup. Here’s a more detailed tutorial on downgrading from the macOS beta and we also have a tutorial on downgrading to an older version of the Mac OS.

9.

Is the beta free to download? 


Yes, the macOS beta is free to download for both developers and the general public. Apple offers two distinct tracks for testing pre-release software: the Developer Beta and the Public Beta, both of which are now accessible without a paid subscription.

10.

Can I go back to the stable version?

Yes, you can go back to the stable version of macOS from a beta, but the complexity of the process depends on whether the final version of that software has been released yet.

If you are running macOS 27.2 beta and want to return to the current public release of macOS 27, simply turning off Beta Updates will stop future beta installations, but it will not immediately downgrade the Mac. To return before Apple releases an equivalent public build, you may need to erase the Mac and reinstall macOS, then restore data from a backup made before installing the beta.

11.

Should I install the beta on my main Mac?

Installing a macOS beta on your primary computer is generally not recommended due to the inherent risks of using unfinished software. While beta programs offer early access to new features, they are designed for testing and often contain significant bugs that can disrupt your daily workflow.

12.

Do I need an Apple Developer account to install the beta?

You do not need a paid Apple Developer account to install the macOS beta. While access to developer betas was previously restricted to those paying a $99/£79 annual fee, Apple changed this policy in 2023 to allow anyone with a free developer account to access these builds. Alternatively, you can join the Public Beta program, which is also free and accessible to anyone with a valid Apple ID.

13.

How often are new beta versions released?

New macOS beta versions are typically released every one to two weeks, with the frequency increasing as the final public release date approaches. The beta updates refine features and address bugs identified by testers.

14.

Is the macOS beta safe to install?

The beta is generally safe to test, but it may contain bugs that cause crashes, poor battery life, app compatibility issues, or data loss. Always back up your Mac before installing.

15.

Will my apps work with the macOS beta?

Many apps will work normally, but some third-party software may crash, perform poorly, or not launch at all until developers release updates.

Should you install the macOS beta?

Apple

Installing the macOS beta lets you test Apple’s next round of features, fixes and refinements before their public release. Most Mac users should remain on the standard version of macOS 27, particularly if they rely on their Mac for work.

Install if…

  • You need to test apps
  • You want early access to new features
  • You have a secondary Mac available

Wait if…

  • This is your primary work machine
  • You rely on niche or specialist software
  • Stability is critical to your workflow

What are the risks of installing beta software?

Installing pre-release software on a primary device carries several risks.

  • System instability: Performance problems, freezes, crashes, and other unexpected behavior are common during beta testing.
  • App failures: Third-party applications may crash, behave unpredictably, or stop working entirely.
  • Hardware strain: Early beta builds can increase battery drain and cause Macs to run hotter than usual.
  • Data loss: Software bugs may corrupt files, and downgrading to a stable version often requires a complete system reset.

Safety precautions and best practices

If you decide to install the beta, take the following precautions:

  • Use a secondary device: Avoid installing beta software on your primary Mac or on any machine used for critical work.
  • Create a full backup: Use Time Machine to create a complete backup before upgrading so you can restore your Mac if something goes wrong. Note that this needs to be a Time Machine backup from before the beta was installed and you will lose anything saved subsequently.
  • Install on a separate volume: Consider installing the beta on a separate volume or external SSD rather than replacing your main operating system.
  • Check storage space: Make sure you have at least 15GB of free storage available before beginning the installation.

FAQ

1.

Who can run the macOS beta?

Anyone can run the macOS beta, but to do so, you do need to register for either the developer beta, the public beta, or both.

Apple offers both developer and public beta programs for macOS, enabling all interested users to test pre-release versions of the operating system. While both betas provide early access to new features, they cater to different user profiles based on technical expertise and risk tolerance. Beta software tends to be buggy so the more stable public beta version may be preferable, but even that will not be bug-free.

In the past, the developer beta was only available to developers who had paid to join Apple’s Developer Program (which costs $99/£79). However, for a couple of years now, Apple has opened up the developer beta to registered developers with free developer accounts. We explain how to get a free developer account below.

If you decide you no longer want to run the beta version of macOS read this: How to remove the macOS beta.

2.

macOS public beta vs developer beta

Since 2023, the Developer Beta has been available to anyone who registers as a developer, even if they aren’t a paid-up member of Apple’s Developer Program. As a result, people with a basic free developer account can download the new macOS developer beta (we show you how to register below).

Whether you should download the developer beta if you aren’t a developer is another question. We don’t recommend you install the developer beta if you aren’t a developer. Instead, our recommendation is to use the public beta (the first version of which usually arrives in July).

There are a few differences between the public and developer betas. The public beta is not the same as the beta that is released through the developer program. The public beta typically launches after the developer beta has undergone initial testing and refinement

Developers get updates to their beta first, and possibly more frequently. But you should keep in mind that betas are by nature not stable, and because the public beta comes after the developer beta it could be a little safer to install.

The most significant difference is probably the motive of the testers: Developers usually have the aim of ensuring their apps work when the updated macOS is released to the general public, while public beta testers are essentially helping Apple detect bugs and offering feedback on the features. Because of this, developers may get to test new features not available in the public beta. 

If you want to get the public beta the first thing you need to do, if you haven’t already, is join Apple’s beta programs read this for more information: How to become an Apple beta tester.

3.

Is the macOS beta stable?

By its nature, a beta has the potential to be unstable. Therefore, it’s not advised that you install it on a Mac that you rely on. If you have a second Mac that isn’t mission-critical, then install it there. We strongly recommend that you don’t risk all by putting the macOS beta on your primary Mac, especially not in the early days of the beta development. 

If you don’t have a second Mac, there are a couple of ways you could run macOS beta on your Mac without running the risk of losing data or finding your Mac stops working:

  • We recommend installing it on a partition, which these days is really a volume (and is much easier to create than a partition was). Read about how to do that here: How to dual-boot Mac: Run two versions of macOS on a Mac.
  • Alternatively, you could install the macOS beta on an external drive and run it on that.

We discuss the safety of the macOS beta and the risks you might be taking in more detail in a separate article.

4.

How to prepare your Mac for the beta

Update your software: We recommend you have the latest full version of macOS installed, although Apple says that the macOS Developer Beta Access Utility requires macOS 10.8 or later.

Make space: We’d recommend at least 25-30GB of available space because the macOS betas tend to be very large. If you end up requiring more space, read: How to free up space on Mac. Note that we always recommend that you have at least 10% space free on your Mac at any time, so if you don’t have that, expect problems!

Back up: Before you install a beta on your Mac, you should make a backup of your data and files. You can find out how to use Time Machine to back up your Mac. We also have a round-up of suitable backup solutions.

5.

How to send feedback to Apple

Should you come across an error or a bug, you should use the Feedback Assistant app to provide feedback to Apple. Launch the app and follow the appropriate steps, selecting the area about which you’re providing feedback and then any specific sub-area. Then describe your issue in a single sentence, before providing a more detailed description, including any specific steps that reproduce the issue. You’ll also be able to attach other files.

You’ll also have to give permission for the Feedback Assistant app to collect diagnostic information from your Mac.

It won’t always be obvious whether something is a bug or just not as easy to use as you might have hoped. Either way, if your feedback is that something appears to work in an illogical way, Apple will want to know that.

If you are having trouble with a third-party app, you can let Apple know by reporting it through the 3rd-party Application Compatibility category in the Feedback Assistant. However, we’d suggest that you also provide feedback to the app’s developer, who will no doubt be grateful.

6.

Will I be able to update from macOS beta to the final version?

Beta users can move to the finished release once its build is newer than – or equivalent to – the beta installed. Read: How to leave the macOS beta.

7.

Can I talk about the beta publicly?

According to Apple and the license agreement all beta testers must agree to, the beta is “Apple confidential information”. By accepting those terms, you agree not to discuss your use of the software with anyone who isn’t also in the Beta Software Program. That means you can’t “blog, post screenshots, tweet, or publicly post information about the public beta software.”

However, you can discuss any information that Apple has publicly disclosed; the company says that information is no longer considered confidential.

8.

How to downgrade from the macOS beta

You can always revert to an earlier version of macOS, though depending on how you back up, it’s not necessarily a painless process.

Start by making sure the data on your drive is backed up, then erase the drive and install the latest public version of macOS. When you first start up your Mac, you can use the Migration Assistant to import your data from the backup. Here’s a more detailed tutorial on downgrading from the macOS beta and we also have a tutorial on downgrading to an older version of the Mac OS.

9.

Is the beta free to download? 


Yes, the macOS beta is free to download for both developers and the general public. Apple offers two distinct tracks for testing pre-release software: the Developer Beta and the Public Beta, both of which are now accessible without a paid subscription.

10.

Can I go back to the stable version?

Yes, you can go back to the stable version of macOS from a beta, but the complexity of the process depends on whether the final version of that software has been released yet.

If you are running macOS 27.2 beta and want to return to the current public release of macOS 27, simply turning off Beta Updates will stop future beta installations, but it will not immediately downgrade the Mac. To return before Apple releases an equivalent public build, you may need to erase the Mac and reinstall macOS, then restore data from a backup made before installing the beta.

11.

Should I install the beta on my main Mac?

Installing a macOS beta on your primary computer is generally not recommended due to the inherent risks of using unfinished software. While beta programs offer early access to new features, they are designed for testing and often contain significant bugs that can disrupt your daily workflow.

12.

Do I need an Apple Developer account to install the beta?

You do not need a paid Apple Developer account to install the macOS beta. While access to developer betas was previously restricted to those paying a $99/£79 annual fee, Apple changed this policy in 2023 to allow anyone with a free developer account to access these builds. Alternatively, you can join the Public Beta program, which is also free and accessible to anyone with a valid Apple ID.

13.

How often are new beta versions released?

New macOS beta versions are typically released every one to two weeks, with the frequency increasing as the final public release date approaches. The beta updates refine features and address bugs identified by testers.

14.

Is the macOS beta safe to install?

The beta is generally safe to test, but it may contain bugs that cause crashes, poor battery life, app compatibility issues, or data loss. Always back up your Mac before installing.

15.

Will my apps work with the macOS beta?

Many apps will work normally, but some third-party software may crash, perform poorly, or not launch at all until developers release updates.

Earlier this year, when other rival companies were slowly raising prices due to RAM and storage shortages, we praised Apple for keeping things steady, but when the price hikes arrived in June, they were brutal. Products released since then, including the iPhone 18 Pro and M6 Mac mini, have seen additional price hikes, and there are numerous clues that further price hikes are a distinct possibility.

In an otherwise celebratory earnings call this week, for instance, hints were dropped about recent increases in component costs, and what they might mean for Apple’s pricing in the future.

Over the course of the call (for ease of reference, I’m working from Jason Snell’s transcript over on Six Colors), Apple CFO Kevan Parekh used the phrase “higher memory costs” four times and “memory impact” twice; he also, as a bonus, said, “We expect the memory costs to continue to be a challenge for us.” New CEO John Ternus, meanwhile, spoke about the topic at some length, describing current memory pricing as “unprecedented,” then predicting “even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors” in the December quarter followed by still more increases in the quarters beyond.

Given those predictions, and Apple’s citation of higher memory costs as the reason for the original price hikes, it seems logical to expect Apple products to continue to get more expensive in the short to medium term. But the company was reluctant to admit this in so many words.

Wamsi Mohan, a representative of Bank of America, posed a question about this at the earnings call: “Is Apple changing anything in the way that you are procuring memory?” he asked. “How do you think about the progression of memory over time? And if it continues to be a headwind, is pricing also going to remain dynamic [and] potentially move higher?”

This, I’m afraid, is a classic journalistic mistake: the multi-part question which allows the respondent to answer only the parts they like. And cynical readers will be unsurprised to hear that Apple COO Sabih Khan chose to focus on the altogether less awkward first two parts and ignore the third. He talked about supplier relationships and purchase obligations and left it at that.

But that wasn’t the end of the matter. Perhaps Kevan Parekh figured that, if that was all the answer he received, Mohan would use his follow-up to drill down into the pricing issue some more and it would look like Apple had dodged the question. So he addressed it… after a fashion.

“Wamsi, maybe I’ll add here because you asked the question about pricing and how we’re managing it,” he began. “So look, we’re trying to manage this with a number of actions.

“You were just talking about the fact we’re continuing to pursue lower cost in non-memory components. John mentioned the fact that we have some benefit of carry-in inventory, and we did reluctantly make the decision to change pricing on a number of our products, starting with the iPad and Mac in the June timeframe and then iPhone more recently in September. I think what we try to do, in doing all that, we evaluate the unit’s revenue and margin, and we’re really being thoughtful and deliberate at evaluating kind of the short-term and long-term considerations, and I believe we’re balancing this well.”

In other words, Apple looks at the revenue and margin of a product and then acts accordingly, trying to balance short- and long-term considerations. (I’m putting words in Parekh’s mouth here, but I take that to mean balancing the short-term harm of reduced profit against the long-term harm of lower sales and a smaller install base to sell services and accessories into.) Which is fairly obvious and doesn’t offer a great deal of new information.

So the official answer on the subject of Apple price rises is… we will act in a “thoughtful and deliberate way.” But we’ve heard that before, and reading between the lines of all the complaints about memory costs in the rest of the earnings call, it’s looking increasingly likely that Apple will have to push up pricing again.

It’s been two years since the last iPad mini was released, which sported a design that was introduced in 2021. Over a short amount of time, the iPad mini (A17 Pro) became a package with a dated chip, display, and design.

Enter the iPad mini (A20 Pro). With this update, Apple gave its smallest tablet a complete overhaul: its latest A-series chip, a sparkling new OLED display, and a more compact design. While it might look the same at a glance, spend a little time with it, and you’ll see just how different it is.

It’s an update that comes at the right time. With prices on the rise (and no ceiling in sight), the $699 iPad mini finds itself in an appealing spot, offering an impressive combination of features and performance for the price.

A20 Pro iPad mini: Design

A large part of Apple’s design philosophy is to make its products as compact as possible, especially with its portable devices. Even the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is thinner than the previous model.

That treatment is especially true if the product has “mini” in its name. Take, for example, the history of the Mac mini, particularly the recent 2024 Mac mini redesign. This time, it’s the iPad mini’s turn, and it’s now the most compact iPad mini Apple has made.  Here’s how the new iPad mini compares in size to the old one.

The iPad mini (A20 Pro) is the same height as before, but it’s a bit narrower, thinner, and lighter. It’s smaller all around, which makes it more comfortable to hold in one hand, and you might even forget it’s in your bag. The previous iPad mini was small enough for me to always have in my backpack, but it pushed the border of pocketability. The new iPad mini’s slight reduction in size is a better fit for cargo pants pockets and smaller carryalls.

The new iPad mini is the first iPad to have an Ingress Protection (IP) rating. In this case, its IP67 rating means it has a dust protection rating of 6, the highest rating, while the water resistance rating is 7 (out of 9), which means the iPad mini should survive being submerged in about 3 feet of water for up to 30 minutes. Besides individual consumer use outside, I’ve often seen the iPad mini used at outdoor events by staff, so the IP67 construction is an excellent idea to protect their investment.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

A20 Pro iPad mini: OLED Display

The major upgraded component of the iPad mini (A20 Pro) is the display, which now has OLED (Super Retina XDR) that replaces the LED-backlit IPS (Liquid Retina) panel. It’s not the tandem OLED that’s in the iPad Pro, so its overall image quality doesn’t compare to that particular device.

But compared to the iPad mini (A17 Pro), the difference is noticeable and improved. The new iPad mini is rated at 600 nits for SDR and XDR brightness, 100 nits brighter than before. And the new iPad mini can hit a peak of 1,200 nits when viewing HDR content, something the old iPad mini couldn’t do. It’s a difference you can especially appreciate when, say, you’re using the iPad mini in direct sunlight–it made lounging in my backyard on a sunny Sunday afternoon much more pleasurable.

OLED is a better technology than LED-backlit, so everything looks better: the Home screen, apps, text, graphics, even the surrounding white spaces in Photos. As for the photos themselves, the colors are more vivid, and the contrast is more discernible.

The one disappointment about the display is its 60Hz refresh rate. Apple’s standard 60Hz dfisplays are better than most, but it would’ve been nice if the mini had ProMotion, Apple’s variable refresh rate feature that goes up to 120Hz. Faster refresh rates make videos and animations look smoother, and video games benefit greatly. ProMotion used to be a feature just for Pro devices until Apple added it to the iPhone 17.

Roman Loyola/Macworld

ProMotion seems like a perfect fit for the iPad mini, often used as an entertainment device, where a faster rate makes videos and high-end games look smoother. Apple will probably add it to the next iPad mini, but it’s going to be a while before that model arrives, since the iPad mini is on a longer product cycle (2 to 3 years).

Finally, the bezels on the new mini are also quite a bit thinner, and it’s striking how dated the A17 Pro iPad mini looks now. The thinner bezels help the new iPad mini eke out a larger 8.5-inch viewable area, compared to the previous 8.3 inches. Also, the bezels around the corners are more rounded and more in harmony with the outer corners of the iPad mini itself compared to the squarer A17 Pro iPad mini’s bezels.

A20 Pro iPad mini: Speakers

For the first time ever, Apple has made an iPad without speakers. Or rather, without speaker holes. The iPad mini’s new Acoustic Display is a sound system comprised of tweeters between the glass-and-aluminum enclosure, and woofers paired through the display.

Essentially, the sound from the iPad mini A20 Pro feels like it emanates through the glass–hold the iPad mini’s display to your ear, and you can hear the sound coming through. It makes a profound difference in the aural experience and gives the illusion that you’re in the song rather than just listening to it. By comparison, the iPad mini with speaker grills projects sound outward instead of toward you, creating something of a disconnect between you and the device.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

As for the actual sound quality, I had a difficult time hearing the difference between the old and new iPad minis. It sounds better and clearer than the iPhone 18 Pro Max speaker, though the sound is still tinny and missing depth. Bass is improved, but not by much; one of my favorite songs to play for bass is Public Enemy’s “Shut ‘Em Down,” and its bassline is a shadow of what’s heard through high-quality speakers.

A20 Pro iPad mini: Processor upgrades

There’s a three-year gap between the A20 Pro in the new iPad and the A17 Pro it replaces. That means the performance improvements are quite noticeable, at least from a benchmark standpoint.

The single-core CPU result shows a 51 percent performance increase with the A20 Pro. This means that you’ll notice a difference with a majority of apps you use on the new iPad mini: productivity tasks, social media apps, communication tools, browsers, casual games, consumer-level creative software, and a lot more. In everyday, general usage, the iPad A20 Pro feels snappy, quick, and up to the task.

Multi-core CPU results show a similar improvement of 50 percent. That’s also impressive, but since the iPad mini isn’t usually used as a production tool like the iPad Pro (or even the iPad Air), most customers won’t feel these benefits nearly as much.

If you do happen to use the iPad mini to do a lot of graphical work or play a lot of high-end games, you’ll like what the A20 Pro has to offer. Its GPU performance is excellent and is leaps and bounds better than the A17 Pro, a 180 percent jump in performance.  That’s a lot for the iPad mini, but to put it in perspective, Apple released the A18 Pro and A19 Pro in the meantime, so the A20 Pro’s result includes a cumulative effect from those chips.

A20 Pro iPad mini: Battery life

Apple’s new iPhone Duo is both big and small, and it’s more susceptible to knocks and drops than a standard iPhone with its folding function maybe taking a while to get used to. It’s the first iPhone that needs a case built around moving parts—namely the hinge. A case for a foldable can be made from one or two shells, with the additional question of covering the hinge or leaving it bare. The phone goes on sale October 23, and cases are already arriving.

iPhone Duo test criteria

We look for eight key criteria when testing each case.

Simon Jary

Protection: We checked corner reinforcement, camera and screen-edge protection, hinge coverage, and how much of the handset each shell covers. We did not run our own drop tests, so protection assessments are based on construction and coverage, and we note manufacturer claims as claims. Some case makers specify the exact measurements of their raised screen and camera edges, other do not.

Materials and grip: We assess surface texture, grip, finish, and visible fingerprint marks during handling. Common case materials include TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane, a flexible, durable plastic) and aramid fiber (a lightweight, high-strength synthetic fiber, best known through the Kevlar brand). The material alone does not establish how well a case protects the phone; construction and coverage also matter. Long-term wear, discoloration, and adhesive durability cannot be established during these initial checks.

Hinge protection and operation: Cases take different approaches to the Duo’s hinge: some include a protective cover, while others leave it exposed. We opened and closed each case on the dummy handset, checking for stiffness, rattling, gaps, and smooth movement of any hinge cover. We also checked whether both shells stayed firmly attached during opening and closing. These checks provide an initial assessment of the case’s construction and movement. We will assess the effect on the actual phone’s hinge movement or opening angle will require further testing with a working iPhone Duo.

Fit and installation: We used the dummy iPhone Duo to assess how securely each section fits the handset, the alignment of cutouts, and the ease of installation. We also checked the positioning and accessibility of button covers and port openings. Final fit and tolerances, button response, Touch ID operation, and cable fit will need confirmation with a retail iPhone Duo.

Slimness: The Duo’s thin profile is part of its appeal but this must be weighed against the backplate’s coverage and reinforcement. We penalize cases that add bulk without a clear benefit, but not where the protective benefits are worthwhile.

Extra functions: Some iPhone Duo cases include a kickstand for easier viewing. We assessed adjustability and how much bulk the stand adds. ESR’s Flex Stand, for example, rotates 180° and forms a protective guard around the camera bar when not in use. Other stands, such as those on the Torras Ostand and UAG Mouve XTE, rotate 360° and fold flat against the case backplate. The Moft Dynamic Folio uses an origami-like folding stand. Stability with a working iPhone Duo, both folded and unfolded, will require further testing because its weight and balance may differ from those of the dummy handset.

Colors and style: We assessed the range of colors and the quality of the finishes provided. Most of the color and pattern will be seen on the case’s backplate, but it should also be noticed on the front frame and hinge protector where present.

Magnetic accessory compatibility: We checked how securely magnetic chargers, power banks, wallets, and other accessories attached, and whether the case’s camera surround, hinge protection, or kickstand obstructed their fit. Because we used a dummy handset for our initial testing, these checks assess attachment and clearance only. We will test charging performance—including speed, heat, and reliability—once we have a working iPhone Duo.

FAQ

Does the iPhone Duo need a case?

No phone needs a protective case until you drop or knock it. A case isn’t essential for the iPhone Duo, but it’s a sensible investment for a $1,999 foldable. Apple’s Ceramic Shield glass helps protect the displays, but the titanium edges and hinge remain vulnerable to accidental drops, scratches and dents. Unlike conventional iPhone cases, Duo designs must accommodate two halves and a slim cover-screen frame, often using adhesive to stay securely attached.

What to consider when choosing an iPhone Duo case?

Prioritize a precise fit, shock-absorbing corners and the level of coverage you think you need. Raised lips help protect the exterior display and camera, while a dedicated hinge guard covers the folding spine. Check that the case allows easy access to Touch ID and Camera Control without obstructing the inner display or folding mechanism. Since the Duo already weighs 8.9oz (254g), consider whether extra bulk from a kickstand or hinge protector is worthwhile. Choose a slim two-piece case for everyday protection or a hinge-cover design for additional coverage.

Will a case interfere with the iPhone Duo’s hinge or folding action?

A properly fitted iPhone Duo case shouldn’t interfere with folding, but poorly designed hinge covers can add bulk or restrict movement. Some two-piece cases leave the hinge exposed; others include a separate hinge cover, while dedicated covers provide an additional barrier against knocks and grit. However, hinge coverage doesn’t necessarily mean dust protection. Debris can collect between the case and phone, so remove the case periodically and gently clean both surfaces according to Apple’s care guidance. For cases secured with adhesive strips, follow the manufacturer’s removal and cleaning instructions, and check whether replacement strips are required before refitting.

Can I remove and reuse an iPhone Duo case?

That depends on how the case attaches. Some iPhone Duo cases use adhesive strips to secure the front frame or other components. Don’t assume those strips will retain their grip after removal: check whether the manufacturer allows reuse, supplies spare strips, or sells replacements.

A removable component isn’t necessarily reusable with the same adhesive. Before taking off an adhesive-mounted case for cleaning or swapping cases, follow its removal instructions and check what you’ll need to refit it securely.

Is a kickstand case necessary for the iPhone Duo?

If you regularly watch videos, make FaceTime calls or use your iPhone Duo for work, a kickstand case is a useful upgrade. It props up the larger inner display for hands-free viewing, video calls, recipes, and reading. Paired with a Bluetooth keyboard, it can also support light productivity. Some stands double as finger grips for safer handling. The main drawback is added thickness and weight, so look for a stable, well-integrated design that folds flat to the backplate or doubles as a camera bar.

Will MagSafe chargers, wallets, and power banks fit with these cases?

MagSafe uses magnets to align and attach compatible wireless chargers, power banks, wallets, and other accessories. The cases listed here are described as MagSafe compatible, but that doesn’t guarantee every accessory will fit.

Because the iPhone Duo is shorter than a conventional iPhone, larger magnetic wireless power banks and wallets may extend beyond its edges or overlap the camera bar. A case’s kickstand or hinge cover may also prevent an accessory from sitting flat or interfere with unfolding the phone.

Before buying, check the accessory’s dimensions and the case maker’s compatibility guidance. With the accessory attached, make sure it clears the cameras and allows the Duo to open fully. Some wallets and power banks may need to be removed before unfolding.

Our initial case assessments used a dummy handset, allowing us to assess physical clearance and attachment, but not wireless charging performance. We’ll add charging results and recommendations for specific accessories after testing them on a working iPhone Duo.

Would I do better getting AppleCare+ instead of a case?

A combination of slim case and AppleCare+ can offer a good balance between preserving the Duo’s design and protecting against costly accidents. A case helps prevent everyday scratches and knocks, while AppleCare+ covers eligible damage under the plan’s terms, subject to service fees. Theft and loss protection may also be available with a suitable plan. Check Apple’s current pricing and conditions before buying. For maximum peace of mind, use both: prevention for everyday mishaps and coverage for expensive repairs.

iPhone Duo test criteria

We look for eight key criteria when testing each case.

Simon Jary

Protection: We checked corner reinforcement, camera and screen-edge protection, hinge coverage, and how much of the handset each shell covers. We did not run our own drop tests, so protection assessments are based on construction and coverage, and we note manufacturer claims as claims. Some case makers specify the exact measurements of their raised screen and camera edges, other do not.

Materials and grip: We assess surface texture, grip, finish, and visible fingerprint marks during handling. Common case materials include TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane, a flexible, durable plastic) and aramid fiber (a lightweight, high-strength synthetic fiber, best known through the Kevlar brand). The material alone does not establish how well a case protects the phone; construction and coverage also matter. Long-term wear, discoloration, and adhesive durability cannot be established during these initial checks.

Hinge protection and operation: Cases take different approaches to the Duo’s hinge: some include a protective cover, while others leave it exposed. We opened and closed each case on the dummy handset, checking for stiffness, rattling, gaps, and smooth movement of any hinge cover. We also checked whether both shells stayed firmly attached during opening and closing. These checks provide an initial assessment of the case’s construction and movement. We will assess the effect on the actual phone’s hinge movement or opening angle will require further testing with a working iPhone Duo.

Fit and installation: We used the dummy iPhone Duo to assess how securely each section fits the handset, the alignment of cutouts, and the ease of installation. We also checked the positioning and accessibility of button covers and port openings. Final fit and tolerances, button response, Touch ID operation, and cable fit will need confirmation with a retail iPhone Duo.

Slimness: The Duo’s thin profile is part of its appeal but this must be weighed against the backplate’s coverage and reinforcement. We penalize cases that add bulk without a clear benefit, but not where the protective benefits are worthwhile.

Extra functions: Some iPhone Duo cases include a kickstand for easier viewing. We assessed adjustability and how much bulk the stand adds. ESR’s Flex Stand, for example, rotates 180° and forms a protective guard around the camera bar when not in use. Other stands, such as those on the Torras Ostand and UAG Mouve XTE, rotate 360° and fold flat against the case backplate. The Moft Dynamic Folio uses an origami-like folding stand. Stability with a working iPhone Duo, both folded and unfolded, will require further testing because its weight and balance may differ from those of the dummy handset.

Colors and style: We assessed the range of colors and the quality of the finishes provided. Most of the color and pattern will be seen on the case’s backplate, but it should also be noticed on the front frame and hinge protector where present.

Magnetic accessory compatibility: We checked how securely magnetic chargers, power banks, wallets, and other accessories attached, and whether the case’s camera surround, hinge protection, or kickstand obstructed their fit. Because we used a dummy handset for our initial testing, these checks assess attachment and clearance only. We will test charging performance—including speed, heat, and reliability—once we have a working iPhone Duo.

FAQ

Does the iPhone Duo need a case?

No phone needs a protective case until you drop or knock it. A case isn’t essential for the iPhone Duo, but it’s a sensible investment for a $1,999 foldable. Apple’s Ceramic Shield glass helps protect the displays, but the titanium edges and hinge remain vulnerable to accidental drops, scratches and dents. Unlike conventional iPhone cases, Duo designs must accommodate two halves and a slim cover-screen frame, often using adhesive to stay securely attached.

What to consider when choosing an iPhone Duo case?

Prioritize a precise fit, shock-absorbing corners and the level of coverage you think you need. Raised lips help protect the exterior display and camera, while a dedicated hinge guard covers the folding spine. Check that the case allows easy access to Touch ID and Camera Control without obstructing the inner display or folding mechanism. Since the Duo already weighs 8.9oz (254g), consider whether extra bulk from a kickstand or hinge protector is worthwhile. Choose a slim two-piece case for everyday protection or a hinge-cover design for additional coverage.

Will a case interfere with the iPhone Duo’s hinge or folding action?

A properly fitted iPhone Duo case shouldn’t interfere with folding, but poorly designed hinge covers can add bulk or restrict movement. Some two-piece cases leave the hinge exposed; others include a separate hinge cover, while dedicated covers provide an additional barrier against knocks and grit. However, hinge coverage doesn’t necessarily mean dust protection. Debris can collect between the case and phone, so remove the case periodically and gently clean both surfaces according to Apple’s care guidance. For cases secured with adhesive strips, follow the manufacturer’s removal and cleaning instructions, and check whether replacement strips are required before refitting.

Can I remove and reuse an iPhone Duo case?

That depends on how the case attaches. Some iPhone Duo cases use adhesive strips to secure the front frame or other components. Don’t assume those strips will retain their grip after removal: check whether the manufacturer allows reuse, supplies spare strips, or sells replacements.

A removable component isn’t necessarily reusable with the same adhesive. Before taking off an adhesive-mounted case for cleaning or swapping cases, follow its removal instructions and check what you’ll need to refit it securely.

Is a kickstand case necessary for the iPhone Duo?

If you regularly watch videos, make FaceTime calls or use your iPhone Duo for work, a kickstand case is a useful upgrade. It props up the larger inner display for hands-free viewing, video calls, recipes, and reading. Paired with a Bluetooth keyboard, it can also support light productivity. Some stands double as finger grips for safer handling. The main drawback is added thickness and weight, so look for a stable, well-integrated design that folds flat to the backplate or doubles as a camera bar.

Will MagSafe chargers, wallets, and power banks fit with these cases?

MagSafe uses magnets to align and attach compatible wireless chargers, power banks, wallets, and other accessories. The cases listed here are described as MagSafe compatible, but that doesn’t guarantee every accessory will fit.

Because the iPhone Duo is shorter than a conventional iPhone, larger magnetic wireless power banks and wallets may extend beyond its edges or overlap the camera bar. A case’s kickstand or hinge cover may also prevent an accessory from sitting flat or interfere with unfolding the phone.

Before buying, check the accessory’s dimensions and the case maker’s compatibility guidance. With the accessory attached, make sure it clears the cameras and allows the Duo to open fully. Some wallets and power banks may need to be removed before unfolding.

Our initial case assessments used a dummy handset, allowing us to assess physical clearance and attachment, but not wireless charging performance. We’ll add charging results and recommendations for specific accessories after testing them on a working iPhone Duo.

Would I do better getting AppleCare+ instead of a case?

A combination of slim case and AppleCare+ can offer a good balance between preserving the Duo’s design and protecting against costly accidents. A case helps prevent everyday scratches and knocks, while AppleCare+ covers eligible damage under the plan’s terms, subject to service fees. Theft and loss protection may also be available with a suitable plan. Check Apple’s current pricing and conditions before buying. For maximum peace of mind, use both: prevention for everyday mishaps and coverage for expensive repairs.

Apple’s new PROLED XDR display on the MacBook Pro isn’t just the best screen Apple has ever put in a laptop. It’s one of the greatest displays ever made.

When we heard rumors of Apple putting a tandem OLED display in the MacBook Pro, we assumed it would be similar to the iPad Pro’s Ultra Retina XDR display:

  • Wide color (P3)
  • SDR brightness: 1000 nits max
  • XDR brightness: 1000 nits max full screen, 1600 nits peak (HDR content only)
  • 1 nit minimum brightness
  • 2,000,000:1 contrast ratio

Those are excellent specs, of course. The iPad Pro has one of the best displays ever put in a tablet, and surpasses the Liquid Retina XDR mini-LED display in the non-touchscreen MacBook Pro, which is no slouch. They both have high-end features including ProMotion, True Tone, and 3K resolution, but the tandem OLED’s rich, deep colors, and uniform brightness is a clear standout.

I would’ve been plenty happy with those specs. Anyone who’s used an M4 or M5 iPad Pro knows that Apple’s claims of it being the world’s most advanced display are pretty spot on. But the Ultra Retina XDR display in the MacBook Pro is on a whole other level.

As Apple often does with new display technology, it’s published a white paper that describes each of the display’s features and specs, and summarizes the important technologies:

PROLED XDR display on MacBook Pro comprises many innovative, Apple-designed components that are tightly integrated, combined with extremely precise factory calibration, to produce unparalleled front-of-screen performance in a pro laptop. The tandem OLED panel—two stacked electroluminescent-emitting layers—delivers an extraordinary 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, up to 2000 nits of peak brightness, and self-emissive pixels that eliminate the blooming and halo artifacts introduced by other display technologies. And the entire panel is driven by the display engine in M5 Pro and M5 Max, which continuously compensates every pixel in real time for content, usage, temperature, and ambient conditions. An industry-leading low-reflectivity panel design and antireflective coating on the cover glass minimize distracting reflections, and a rigid stiffener keeps the panel perfectly flat to maintain uniformity and prevent mechanical distortion.

That’s very similar to the equivalent passage in the Studio Display XDR’s white paper. In fact, the PROLED XDR in the MacBook Pro is the only display other than the Studio Display XDR that supports Apple CMF 2026, the next generation of CIE 1931. Apple says CMF 2026 “more precisely aligns the appearance of the display with an ideal D65 illuminant—the standard reference for white—and significantly improves appearance matching across display technologies, which is important for workflows that use multiple displays side by side.” The only other display in the world that supports this color mode is the Studio Display XDR, which starts at $2,800 without a stand. 

Apple’s new PROLED XDR doesn’t have anywhere near the 5K resolution of the Studio Display (and doesn’t really need it), but it has the same sustained SDR and HDR brightness, color gamut, and an insane 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, 10 times that of the Studio Display XDR. It also supports medical imaging with 16 reference modes (versus just 11 with the standard MacBook Pro), as well as a display calibrator to fine-tune performance.

There’s a reason why Apple’s new MacBook Pro has such a lengthy name. OLED alone doesn’t do it justice. Neither does XDR. Apple has put an ultra high-end display that would cost thousands on its own inside a laptop for a relatively modest $400 premium. The new MacBook display raises the bar considerably for what a pro laptop can be. 

Oh, and you can also touch it.
